extracted.intended_audience: students of chemistry and practicing chemists (late 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principled rules for classifying substances (acids, bases, metals, terres), naming acids and salts by radical and oxygenation degree, and experimental/analytical practices for preparing and characterising these substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acids as 'principes salifiants' (definition and ontological status)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Les acides peuvent donc être regardés comme de véritables principes salifians ... ils sont formés de la réunion de deux principes simples, ou au moins qui se comportent à la manière des principes simples, & ils sont par conséquent ... dans l'ordre des mixtes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat acids as a distinct class formed by the union of an acidifying principle (oxygen) with a particular radical; distinguish acids from salts (which are formed from the union of two mixtes). Note acid properties (e.g., solubility in water) but do not conflate those properties with being a salt. Use this ontological distinction when analysing and naming substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and definition of 'bases salifiables' (what can form neutral salts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bases salifiables are enumerated: La potasse; La soude; L'ammoniaque; La chaux; La magnésie; La baryte; L'alumine; Et toutes les substances métalliques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining possible salts, restrict base candidates to this set of salifiable bases. The text treats alkalis, terrestrial bases, and metals separately because they have different behaviors (e.g., alkalis and terres enter salts directly, metals usually as oxides).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metals dissolve in acids only after oxidation (requirement for metal dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metal cannot dissolve in an acid unless it can be oxidized there; strictly, "les métaux ne sont point dissolubles dans les acides, mais seulement les oxides métalliques."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of metal–acid reactions must account for oxidation steps (removal of oxygen from acid or water). This explains whether effervescence (gas evolution) occurs and predicts whether a given metal will react with a given acid in the metallic state or only after prior oxidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of effervescence and gas evolution during metal dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Effervescence arises because reduction of strongly oxygenated acids (e.g., nitric, sulfuric) liberates gaseous products: nitrous gas with nitric acid; acid sulfureous or hydrogen with sulfuric acid depending on whether acid or water is decomposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the identity of the gas evolved to infer which reagent (acid or water) provided oxygen in the oxidation of the metal. Predict absence of effervescence when the metal is pre-oxidized, or when the acid provides sufficient water to retain gaseous products in solution (e.g., oxygénated muriatic acid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature principle for acids (radical + oxygenation degree)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: give a common generic name 'acide' and differentiate by the radical acidifiable particular to each; indicate different oxygenation degrees by different terminations (e.g., _sulfureux_ vs _sulfurique_).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming newly discovered acids, identify the radical (base acidifiable) and the common acidifying principle (oxygen). Use systematic endings to reflect oxygenation levels so names convey chemical relationships and oxidation states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature principle for salts (name by acid family then base)
rubrics_metrics.description: Name all salts by the acid family they derive from (e.g., _sulfates_, _phosphates_) and then specify the base salifiable (e.g., _sulfate_ de potasse, _sulfate_ de soude). Distinguish salts formed from less-oxygenated acids using a distinct termination (e.g., _sulfites_ vs _sulfates_).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the acid-based family name first, then qualify by the base to uniquely identify salts. This systematic method scales to many combinations and avoids arbitrary historical names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration and classification as a methodological requirement (lists of acids and bases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author compiles a list of 48 known acids (including 17 metallic acids) and states there are 24 bases salifiables (three alkalis, four terres, and seventeen metallic substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain exhaustive, explicit lists of known radicals/acids and known salifiable bases as the foundation for systematic nomenclature and for enumerating possible salts; update lists as discoveries are made but use them for combinatorial reasoning and naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial accounting for salts and need for a systematic method
rubrics_metrics.description: From the counts of acids and bases one may conceive 1152 possible neutral salts (assuming metals can dissolve others); arbitrary, eponymous naming would create confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an analogical, systematic nomenclature (acid-family + base) to manage combinatorial explosion of possible salts; prefer a method that generalises to newly discovered species rather than ad hoc names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental procedure and purification for potash
rubrics_metrics.description: Potash is obtained by lixiviating plant ashes: water charges with potash, evaporate water to obtain fixed potash; potash often saturated with carbonic acid and is purified by dissolving, adding quicklime, filtering, evaporating in closed vessels; pure potash is deliquescent and soluble in alcohol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing or characterising potash, account for its common carbonic acid contamination and use lime treatment to free it; test behaviour (hygroscopicity, solubility in alcohol) as purity indicators. Do not assume raw ash potash is pure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and compositional identification of ammonia
rubrics_metrics.description: Ammoniaque (alkali volatil) is chiefly obtained by distillation of animal matter; Berthollet found ~807 parts nitrogen to 193 hydrogen per 1000 by weight. It is obtained mixed with water, oil, and carbonic acid; purify by first combining with an acid (e.g., muriatic) then liberating by adding lime or potash; pure ammonia exists only as a gas at ordinary temperature and has a very penetrating odour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterise ammonia by its origin (animal distillation), composition (N:H ratio), and phases (aqueous 'ammoniaque en liqueur' vs 'gaz ammoniac'). Purify via acid-salt formation and base-driven liberation; use behaviour on absorption in cold water and effects of pressure/cooling to identify concentrated solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat lesser-understood 'terres' as simple until proven composite
rubrics_metrics.description: The compositions of chaux, magnésie, baryte & alumine are 'absolutely unknown'; until further discoveries, they are to be regarded as simple substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classification and nomenclature, provisionally treat poorly understood earths as elemental/simple. Document this provisional status and be prepared to revise names/classifications when experimental decomposition shows constituent parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic tabulation of substances and combinations (ten-table plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second part proposes ten tables: (1) substances simples; (2) radicals oxidables & acidifiables double & triple; (3) oxygen combinations with simple substances; ... up to (10) combinations of other radicals. These tables recap and systematise prior chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured tables to summarise substances, radicals, and combinations so readers can apply the naming method and find simple routes to prepare acids and predict properties of resulting salts. Place explanations adjacent to tables for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical/experimental rigor recommendation to chemists
rubrics_metrics.description: "...je recommanderai ... de s'attacher plutôt à faire bien qu'à faire beaucoup; à s'assurer d'abord par des expériences précises & multipliées de la composition des acides, avant de s'occuper de celle des sels neutres."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise careful, replicated experiments establishing acid composition before extensive work on salts. Build nomenclature and classification on firm experimental foundations rather than numerous but imprecise reports; quality of data supersedes quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt consistent terminology for 'substances simples' and map new to old terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a table mapping 'Noms nouveaux' (e.g., Lumière, Calorique, Oxygène, Azote, Hydrogène) to 'Noms anciens' (e.g., Chaleur, Air déphlogistiqué, Gaz phlogistiqué, Gaz inflammable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a systematic chemical theory, explicitly map new terminology to historical/common terms to aid comprehension. Use consistent, well-defined names (calorique, oxygène, azote, hydrogène) so subsequent classification and nomenclature remain clear.
